capabilities.title: 1 · Project libraries
capabilities.description: Each project gets its own library, a separate database on one Postgres server, created the first time the project is opened, with its tables set up automatically, and brought up to date by the next open after storytree adds to them. Opening a project whose tables are already current touches no table, so an account let only read, or write a few kinds of record, can open it too. Storytree can list the projects on the server, and nothing written in one project can ever show up in another, with one exception: a product project names the user's factory, and reads its system (roles, notes and checks) from it, its own records of the same kind and title winning (ADR-1040).

contracts.title: 1.1 · `openProject("site")` on a server with no storytree databases creates the project's database and its tables; a project set up before a table changed gains what was added since at its next open.
1.2 · Opening the same project again succeeds and changes nothing (no error, no second database, its records are untouched).
1.3 · After opening "site" and "app", `listProjects()` returns exactly `["app", "site"]`. Databases on the server that are not storytree projects are never listed.
1.4 · A record saved in "site" cannot be read from "app".

1.5 · A project name that is not lower-case letters, digits and single hyphens (1–40 characters, starting with a letter or digit) is refused before anything touches the server, and the error names the rule.
1.6 · `snapshot("site")` returns every record of the project and its whole history, as they stood at one moment, while writes go on.

1.7 · `restore("copy", snapshot)` into a project with no records and no history gives back the same records and the same history, sequence numbers, actors and times included, and the next write continues after them.
1.8 · Restoring into a project that holds any record or any history is refused, naming the project, and writes nothing.

1.9 · A local database that accepts TCP but never completes a fresh handshake is refused at a 10-second connection deadline by default (ADR-1163 D1), or at the deadline the caller gives, for both the server and project pools, with an actionable "storytree isn't reachable" answer that says the database took longer than that to answer and the computer may be busy. This includes library opens made by the CLI. A later call recovers once the database answers.

1.10 · Opening a project whose tables are current runs no table setup and writes nothing, so an account that may only read its tables (not their owner, no right to create in its schema) opens it and reads its records.

1.11 · Opening a project whose tables are not current, as an account that may not change them (no CREATE on its schema, or not holding the owner's rights over its tables), changes nothing: no table statement runs and no memory is converted. A project set up before opens as its tables stand, reads and writes as the account's grants allow, and warns once per process per project, naming the project, the account and the role owning its database. A project never set up is refused with a ConnectionError (`project-owner`) naming the project and the account and saying that only the role owning its database may set it up. Its owner's next open sets the tables up as before.

1.12 · `dropProject(name)` deletes the project's database, with every record and all its history, for every machine using the server; it is listed no more, other projects are untouched, and an unknown project is refused. An open that only reaches an existing project (`openProject(name, { create: false })`, how a folder that names a project opens it) refuses a deleted one as gone and never makes it again.
contracts.description: The library call under deleting a project (ADR-0831). Irreversible: a snapshot taken first is the only way back. Others' connections to the database are ended (DROP DATABASE … WITH (FORCE)).

contracts.title: 1.13 · Closing a server connection waits for project and own-database openings already in flight, releases every pool they create, and refuses new openings once closing starts.
contracts.description: Concurrent callers of close wait for the same cleanup. An opening stalled on real Postgres when shutdown starts cannot return a live pool after shutdown; later reads or opens cannot revive the closed server. Pin with throwaway Postgres connection counts and a held schema-read lock.

reported.note: Both 1.13 regressions now pass against throwaway Postgres; all 42 focused tests pass, including existing Cloud SQL path cap/retry and own-database coverage. Full gate follows.

contracts.title: 1.14 · Loopback database connections refuse cleartext and MD5 password requests before sending credential material, for both admin and project pools; SCRAM and passwordless test connections still work.
1.15 · A project records whether it is the user's factory or a product naming its factory, and refuses to be both
contracts.description: ADR-1040. Kept in the project's own library (library_meta kind and factory): markFactory makes a project the factory (true the first time, false after), recordFactory names a product's factory; a factory naming a factory, a product being made a factory, and a project naming itself are refused and change nothing.

contracts.title: 1.16 · A product project reads its factory's roles, notes and checks, and its own record of the same kind and title wins
contracts.description: A project naming a factory (1.15) reads, from its next opening, the factory's agent roles, principles, guardrails, patterns, processes and checks beside its own, through list, select and get, so every reader (search_notes, open, the review's brief, check_setup) sees them. Its own record of the same kind and title shadows the factory's, also when read by the factory record's id, so a role's links read the product's edits. Memory (decisions and the rest) is never inherited, nothing the product writes reaches the factory, and a product whose factory is gone or is not a factory reads only its own.

contracts.title: 1.17 · A product's link to a system record it retired reads the record of that kind and title: its own, else its factory's
contracts.description: ADR-1040. Moving onto a factory retires a product's unedited copies; get of such a retired id gives the product's live record of the same kind and title, else the factory's, so roles and notes linking the dropped copy keep their links. Retired memory stays retired.

contracts.title: 1.18 · An edit through a product of a system record it reads from its factory writes the product's own copy, which wins, and retiring one hides it from the product; the factory is unchanged
contracts.description: ADR-1040. Copy-on-write: editing a factory record the product holds no copy of creates the product's own copy under the factory's id with the edit applied (an edit through a factory id the product shadows by title edits its shadow); retiring one retires the shadow, if any, and a copy under the factory's id, which hides the factory's record from the product's get and list even after the factory edits it. The factory's records are never written.

contracts.title: 1.19 · A product's inherited records are the factory's system records it reads and holds none of its own for
contracts.description: ADR-1040. inherited() on a product's records gives the factory's roles, notes and checks whose kind and title the product holds no record of, and whose id it never retired a copy under, in id order, read from the factory as it is now; its own copies and shadows, what it retired, and the factory's memory are left out. What a product's globe draws beside its own history.

contracts.title: 1.20 · A local url naming a connect_timeout (libpq's, in seconds) longer than the given deadline gives its handshakes that deadline, on both admin and project pools, and the refusal says so; a url naming none, or a shorter one, keeps the given deadline (10 seconds by default)
contracts.description: How a test run gives its throwaway Postgres room on a loaded machine (increment_223bd1a82663, friction_a10496dd9c49, friction_6c375e8fca6d) without loosening the bound a real library keeps.

contracts.title: 1.21 · A project opened with system switches leaves each switched-off role, check and note out of its lists, selections and searches, a product's factory's included; a record's own title or id beats its group, which beats all; reading one by its id still finds it, and the plan is never switched off
contracts.description: ADR-1092 D2: the library half of the system switches. Filters the merged output only, so a product's own record switched off never lets its factory's same-title record show; a limit counts only what is shown.

contracts.title: 1.22 · Each history entry carries the server's own time and the account that wrote it, and no writer may change or remove one
contracts.description: Every row of a project's history (record_event) carries recorded_at, the server's own time, and recorded_by, the account the server saw, set by the server on every insert whatever the writer sends; the writer's at and actor are kept beside them. An entry written before a project gained these columns keeps them empty. Updating, deleting or truncating the history is refused for every role, the table's owner included; a repair goes only through the logged switch of contract 1.28.

contracts.title: 1.23 · An outside writer's role, fenced to its plugin's kinds, inserts a record of its own kind, and each history entry carries its role in recorded_by
contracts.description: ADR-1178 D1/D5: fenceOutsideWriter, applied as the project database's owner, lets a writer that connects as its own role (voice's storytree_voice first) insert records of its plugin's declared kinds, written as storytree writes them, and read them back; the database's recorded_by stamp names the door each entry came through.

contracts.title: 1.24 · An outside writer's role is refused a core kind, another plugin's kind, an update, a delete and any change to the tables
contracts.description: The template grants only one plugin's dotted kinds; under its row security the role cannot insert a core or another plugin's record, add history under another id, update even its own record when its plugin declares no updates, delete anything, or create, alter or drop a table or policy.

contracts.title: 1.25 · An outside writer whose plugin declares updates may change its own kind's records, and still no other record nor another kind
contracts.description: With update declared, the role may update its own kind's records (record and history), never turn one into another kind or touch a record of a kind it only reads; fencing it again with a narrower grant takes the update and the extra reads back.

contracts.title: 1.26 · A project opened with a plugin's kinds writes and reads them; opened without them, a record of that kind reads dormant
contracts.description: Opened with the kinds the host's mounted factory plugins declare (OpenOptions kinds, ADR-1178 D3), the project creates, gets and lists records of them, its system switches and its factory beside, and refuses fields outside the declared shape; opened without, such a record is read by id as stored and marked dormant, is in no list, and a write of it is refused.

contracts.title: 1.27 · fenceProject fences a plugin's writers in a live project's library as the owner, refusing a missing role or a non-owner account and naming what it fenced first
contracts.description: ADR-1178 D1 and D5. fenceProject reaches project <project>'s database on the server the library setting names (a url or an address; a Cloud SQL library is refused), as the account it signs in as, and fences each writer it is handed in order, each in its own transaction. An account that may not act as the database's owner is refused saying so; a role the server lacks is refused saying it, its LOGIN and its password are made apart from storytree; either way the writers fenced before it stay fenced and are named.

contracts.title: 1.28 · A change to the history goes only through the logged repair switch, for the owner too, and the owner's ordinary writes pass when row-level security is forced
contracts.description: Updating, deleting or truncating record_event is refused for every role, the tables' owner and a superuser included, unless the transaction has turned on the history-repair switch (record_event_repair(reason), the owner's only), which writes each use into history_repair: what was done, why, by which account and when. The switch lasts only for its transaction. With row-level security enabled and forced on record and record_event, the owner's own policies let it read and write records and add history, and not change history without the switch.

contracts.title: 1.29 · A shared library gets schema and own-database table statements only from merged code
contracts.description: A library reached by address or Cloud SQL (a shared one, not the test run's throwaway server) is never given a schema statement that the running code holds only on an unmerged branch: a project set up before opens as it stands with one warning saying why, and one never set up is refused. The same holds for an own database's table statements (ADR-0973): its caller names the modules that declare them, and they are applied to a shared library only when every one is merged; tables naming none count as unmerged there; an own database set up before opens as it stands with one warning, and one never set up is refused. A throwaway library still migrates from the branch. Code counts as merged when it is released: it runs outside a git checkout, or bundled (with no schema file beside it, no module URL of its own, or built into a folder its checkout ignores); or when its declaring file has no uncommitted change and its last commit is on origin/main.

capabilities.title: 2 · Library transactions
capabilities.description: The only data actions the library allows are: save a record, fetch it, list records of one type, change only named fields, retire a record with a reason, revert a record, retired or not, to the state one of its own history entries kept, or revert every record one writer wrote to its state before that writer's first write, refused where another writer wrote since. Every change is all-or-nothing, and is written first to a permanent, append-only history, so nothing is ever truly erased.

contracts.title: 2.1 · `save` creates a record. Saving the same id again replaces it, and each save appends one history entry.
2.2 · `edit` changes only the fields it names; every other field keeps its stored value.
2.3 · `edit` merges onto what is stored NOW, not onto a copy the caller read earlier. If two edits of different fields race, both survive.
2.4 · `edit` of a missing record returns `null` and creates nothing.
2.5 · `get` of a missing record returns `null` and never throws.
2.6 · `list(type)` returns only that type's current records (none retired), and `[]` when there are none.
2.7 · `retire(id, reason)` removes the record from `get`/`list`, keeps the reason in the history, and retiring an already-retired or missing record is a harmless no-op.

2.8 · `history()` returns every change in the order it happened, with strictly increasing sequence numbers. `history({ id })` filters to one record, and `history({ since })` returns only entries after that sequence number.
2.9 · A `validate` check passed to `save`/`edit` sees the merged result. If it throws, nothing is written (no record change and no history entry).

2.10 · A write naming an `actor` keeps it in history. A write without one is accepted and its history entry has no actor; an edit or retirement never inherits an earlier write's actor. Refused writes and harmless no-ops add no history entry.

2.11 · Save, edit and retire accept an optional abort signal. If aborted before write admission, including while waiting for the project write lock, they reject without changing records or history. After admission, cancellation does not interrupt the write or undo its history. The in-memory twin applies the same boundary at write entry.

2.12 · `history` also narrows on the server: `from` (a time) keeps the changes made at or after it, to the millisecond, however the time is written; `types` keeps only changes to records of those types (none for an empty list); `oldest: n` or `newest: n` keeps only the first or last n of what matches, still in order. Filters combine with each other and with `id` and `since`; a malformed one (a limit that is not a whole number above 0, both limits, or a time that is not one) is refused with a RangeError before anything is read.
contracts.description: So a reader that needs one change, or the changes of a few types or since a time, takes only those from the store, not the whole history (arc_0ab31fd59c88, decision_54c045d61591's rule applied to the library's history).

reported.note: memory and postgres behaviour suites pass 2.12

contracts.title: 2.13 · Lists narrow on the server by ids and stored field values, take an ordered limit, and project only requested fields on the named schema version; memory and Postgres agree.
contracts.description: Predicates compare stored JSON scalars before schema upgrades. Projection applies only to its named schema version; other versions arrive whole so SchemaRecords can upgrade without losing source fields or refuse a future version. All SQL paths, values, ids and projection names are parameters.

reported.note: The same transaction behaviour suite passes 22 tests across memory and Postgres, including filtering, ordered limits, nested scalar predicates and version-safe projection.

contracts.title: 2.14 · `revert(id, to, read)` writes the record back to the state its own history entry `to` kept, whole: changed fields restored, removed ones put back, added ones gone. It is one more `updated` entry whose reason names the entry it reverts to, with its writer; nothing in history is rewritten.

2.15 · A revert of a retired record to an entry before its retirement brings it back live under its own id, created when it first was, so links to that id reconnect. A retirement entry is not a state to revert to.

2.16 · A revert is refused, writing nothing, when the record was written to after the entry the writer read (`read` is not its newest seq), when the entry is not the record's own, or when its validate check throws.
2.17 · `history({ actor })` keeps only the changes one writer made, as their entries name them, on the server, combined with the other filters.

2.18 · `revertWrites({ of })` writes every record `of` wrote (health left out) back, in one write, to its state before `of`'s first write to it: a changed record to its entry before, a record `of` retired live again, a record `of` made retired. Each is one more entry naming the writer reverted and the entry it goes back to, with its own writer and reason; a record `of` made and retired itself is left alone. It returns what it changed, by id.

2.19 · `revertWrites` is refused, writing nothing, when another writer (named or not) wrote to any record `of` wrote after `of`'s first write to it: LaterWriterError names each such record with the first such entry and its writer. A check that throws refuses it whole too.
2.20 · A write made for a writer who had read outside text keeps what it read in its history entry; a write without one carries no mark
contracts.description: Each write (save, edit, retire, revert) may name the outside text its writer had read, for a record of a given type; the history entry keeps that list as written, and an entry for a type it names nothing for, or a writer who named none, carries no mark. Observes rather than refuses (increment_572ffca14851, research_fadf5ba21bb6 part 5 item 4).

contracts.title: 2.21 · A library whose history has no place for the outside-text mark yet writes and reads its history as before, leaving the mark off
contracts.description: A shared library takes schema changes only from merged code and an owner's rights, so code with the mark can meet a history table without its column; every write, marked or not, and every history read must still work there (increment_572ffca14851).

contracts.title: 2.22 · Each history entry read back names the account the server saw write it
contracts.description: A history entry read from a Postgres library carries recordedBy, the record_event row's recorded_by (contract 1.22): the account the server saw, whatever actor the writer gave, so a reader can tell which door a record came through (a voice.note written by the door's role storytree_voice, or by the owner's account). Absent for an entry written before the history kept it, and in a store with no server (increment_14f5d05845f5).

capabilities.title: 3 · Data schema
capabilities.description: Every record has a declared type with a fixed set of fields, and a badly filled-in record is refused with a message naming the problem field. Every record is stamped with the schema version it was written on, so a later change to a type is handled deliberately rather than silently misread: an older record is upgraded automatically, step by step, and stored upgraded the next time it is written, because every user's library is their own database and nobody else can repair it.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Saving a `story` with no `title` is refused, the error names `title`, and nothing is written.
3.2 · An unknown field (for example `titel`) is refused and named.
3.3 · An unknown type is refused.
3.4 · Every stored record carries its schema version (1 today).

3.5 · Reading a record stamped with a version newer than this code knows is refused, never guessed at. The error names the record and both schema versions, gives the update and agent-link restart steps, and reports the running code commit distance behind locally fetched origin/main when known; unavailable Git information never masks the refusal or invents a distance.

reported.note: The source-URL guard makes all three code-distance tests pass, including loading the real CommonJS bundle and preserving recovery text with unknown distance.

contracts.title: 3.6 · An `edit` that would leave the record invalid (for example blanking a required field) is refused, and nothing is written.
3.7 · A record written on an OLDER version of its type is read (`get`, `list`) upgraded to the current version, its upgrade steps applied in order. Reading it writes nothing.

3.8 · An `edit` of such a record merges onto its upgraded fields and stores it on the current version, in place, in the same all-or-nothing write. If the upgraded result does not fit, nothing is written.
3.9 · An older record that no upgrade step brings to the next version is refused by `get`, `list` and `edit`, with an error naming the missing step. It is never guessed at.

3.10 · A friction report written before reports carried a state reads with one worked out from its route and stamp (no route open, nothing dismissed, a stamp resolved, any other route routed), and its next write stores it so
contracts.description: Friction's schema version 2 (ADR-1016 D1); the backfill increment settles the rest.

contracts.title: 3.11 · A story and a capability carry their prose as `text`, read back whole and in order; one written without it reads as before
contracts.description: ADR-1050 D1: a story's prose lives in its story, so reading the story returns it.

contracts.title: 3.12 · A process's schedule, time zone and precheck are validated: words the parser cannot read, a grace on any but a daily schedule, an unknown time zone, a precheck not on the fixed list, or a time zone or precheck on a process with no schedule are refused and named

3.13 · A process's schedule reads back as written, and as its rule (a daily schedule's grace in minutes), its times in its own time zone or the owner's, and its precheck as written; a process with no schedule reads as before

capabilities.title: 4 · Work model
capabilities.description: The library holds each project's plan of work: arcs (initiatives), stories (what a user can do), capabilities (the parts that make a story work) and contracts (single testable promises). Capabilities and contracts point at their parent. Stories belong to the project directly, and an arc *may* list the stories it grows, though a research arc may list none. The library refuses broken structure. A capability carries a proposed flag, on from its birth until the agent says it is built (`setProposed`, ADR-0744 D2); switching it says nothing about health, and a capability written before the flag reads proposed. A story is made mapped (ADR-0993 D2) only by mapStories, which an import calls: one mapped story per package of the import, keyed by the package, with no capabilities; a mapped field given to addStory or editStory is refused. A capability of a mapped story is one an agent explored there (ADR-0993 D5): it names the folders and files of its import it covers, inside its story's folders and overlapping no other capability of the story, the refusal naming the one to correct; a capability of a built story covers none.

contracts.title: 4.1 · Add a story, a capability under it and a contract under that, and `projectTree()` returns them nested: story › capability › contract.
4.2 · An arc listing that story is returned by `arcsFor(storyId)`. An arc listing no stories is accepted.
4.3 · A capability naming a missing (or retired) story is refused, as is a contract naming a missing capability and an arc listing a missing story.
4.4 · A capability depending on another capability that does not exist is refused.
4.5 · A dependency loop between capabilities (A → B → A, or longer) is refused, and nothing is written.

4.6 · A capability is born proposed. The agent switches the flag off, and back on, and history names the writer; only a live capability has the flag, and a capability written before the flag reads proposed.

4.7 · A contract planned without a number is given its capability's next free one (after the highest its live contracts carry); a title whose number another live contract of the capability carries is refused, on planning and on correcting, and nothing is written. A capability with no number numbers nothing.

contracts.description: Regression for a contract planned moments after its capability that stayed unnumbered (2026-10-01): contract numbering keys off the capability's stored number.

4.14 · The plan's tree carries a mapped story's import, package and folders as mapStories recorded them; a story storytree built carries none
4.15 · A number given in a contract's title is written in the numbered form, number then " · ", so every reader of contract numbers finds it
contracts.description: addContract and editContract take a title that starts with a contract number followed by its text, with or without the separator ("5.38 Text" or "5.38 · Text"), and store it as "5.38 · Text"; a title that is the number alone, or already carries the separator, is stored as given. CI's health reader and the worklist recognise a contract's number only in that form, so a title stored as "5.38 Text" read "no test names it" though its tests ran (contracts 5.38, 5.39 and 11.18 on 2026-10-11).

contracts.title: 4.16 · a capability on a mapped story is planned with the folders and files of its import it covers, several roots allowed and written plainly; one with none, or a path outside its story's folders, is refused, as are covers on a built story
4.17 · no two capabilities of a mapped story cover one file: a path equal to, inside or around another's is refused, naming the capability that covers it, on planning and on correcting

4.19 · The project's anchor is written a half at a time, what it is and who it is for (setAnchor), at one id, and read back by anchor() and the plan's tree; a half given as undefined is removed, and an empty half is refused with nothing written (ADR-1085 D1).
4.20 · anchorGaps(tree) reads what the plan has not said, the anchor's missing halves only, and nothing when both are said; no story is ever named (ADR-1085 D1, ADR-1096); it fails nothing.

4.21 · a story carries no audience (ADR-1096): one given an audience is refused with nothing written, and one stored with an audience before reads without failing, its tree node carries none, and its next edit stores it without one
4.22 · The plan's tree carries a story's risk reading and guardrails, and a capability's guardrails, as stored; one without them carries none
contracts.description: So the story panel's risk bar can show a story's rating, who it reaches and its extra checks from the tree the app already hands the page (question_1740edf77e9e).

contracts.title: 4.23 · A pull request number resolves through the project's repository cut-over by when it was recorded: before it, the old repository's (none when that one was deleted); on its day or after, the new one's; with no cut-over, the project's one repository's
4.24 · A capability planned or retitled with a number another live capability of its story carries is refused, naming that one and the story's next free number; nothing is written
